title: JEREMIAH CALLED UNFAITHFUL MEN “WELL-FED STALLIONS”—AND WHAT GOD SAW BEHIND THEIR CLOSED DOORS SHOULD TERRIFY US
paragraphs: JEREMIAH CALLED UNFAITHFUL MEN “WELL-FED STALLIONS”—AND WHAT GOD SAW BEHIND THEIR CLOSED DOORS SHOULD TERRIFY US

They had been fed by God, blessed by God, and satisfied by God—yet they were still craving what belonged to someone else. Jeremiah 5:7–8 is not merely an ancient warning about adultery. It is a mirror held in front of the human heart…and the reflection may be closer to us than we want to admit.
There are Bible verses people underline because they comfort them.
There are verses they frame on walls because they inspire them.
And then there are verses like this.
Verses that do not knock politely.
They kick the door open.
They walk into the secret room.
They turn on the light.
And suddenly, the God who sees everything is speaking about what people thought nobody knew.
Jeremiah wrote:
סוּסִים מְיֻזָּנִים מַשְׁכִּים הָיוּ אִישׁ אֶל־אֵשֶׁת רֵעֵהוּ יִצְהָלוּ
Susim meyuzzanim mashkim hayu; ish el-eshet re‘ehu yitzhalu.
The imagery is deliberately humiliating and shocking.
“They were well-fed, lusty stallions, each neighing at another’s wife.” — Jeremiah 5:8

That is essentially what the Hebrew picture communicates, although one of the descriptive Hebrew terms in the verse has some lexical uncertainty, which is why English translations vary slightly in how they render the horses.
But Jeremiah’s central image is unmistakable.
God compares these unfaithful men to horses driven by appetite.
Not husbands protecting covenant.
Not men governing desire.
Not worshipers whose bodies belonged to God.
Stallions.
Fed.
Restless.
Neighing.
Looking over the fence.
Wanting what belonged to somebody else.
And before anyone turns this into an excuse to point at adulterers, pornography addicts, unfaithful spouses, or “those people” in society, there is something uncomfortable we need to understand.
Jeremiah is exposing something much deeper than sexual appetite.
He is exposing the insanity of a heart that has been fed by God and still believes sin has something better to offer.
Read the verse immediately before it.
God says, in essence, that His people abandoned Him, pursued false gods, and then, after He had fed them to fullness, committed adultery.
That sequence matters.
God provided.
They wandered.
God filled.
They lusted.
God remained faithful.
They became unfaithful.
The scandal was not simply that people desired something forbidden.
The scandal was that people who had received so much from God behaved as though God were not enough.
And suddenly Jeremiah 5 does not feel so ancient anymore.
Because you can have food in your refrigerator and still hunger for somebody else's life.
You can have a spouse who loves you and still entertain somebody else's attention.
You can have children calling you Mom or Dad while secretly feeding fantasies that could devastate their home.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday and erase browser history on Monday.
You can know Scripture and still keep a conversation on your phone that you would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
You can say, “God has been good to me,” while secretly negotiating with the very sin that could destroy what His goodness gave you.
You can be full…
and still live hungry.
That is the horror Jeremiah exposes.
The problem was never merely that the horses were hungry.
They were well-fed.
Think about that.
Sometimes our greatest spiritual danger does not arrive when life gives us nothing.
Sometimes it arrives after God has given us much.
Comfort can make us careless.
Blessing can become ordinary.
The spouse you once prayed for becomes familiar.
The home you once dreamed about becomes background scenery.
The ministry opportunity you once begged God for becomes something you take for granted.
The salvation that once brought you to tears becomes vocabulary.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, gratitude becomes entitlement.
Then the fence starts looking interesting.
Someone else's marriage.
Someone else's body.
Someone else's success.
Someone else's possessions.
Someone else's attention.
Someone else's life.
The heart whispers:
Maybe over there.
Maybe happiness is over there.
Maybe excitement is over there.
Maybe fulfillment is over there.
Maybe if I could just have that person…
that experience…
that secret…
that little forbidden thing…
I would finally feel alive again.
And God says:
Look at what sin has reduced you to.
A creature controlled by appetite.
Jeremiah's language is severe because sin is severe.
Adultery is not romantic rebellion.
It breaks covenants.
It devastates spouses.
It confuses children.
It fractures trust.
It can leave wounds people carry for decades.
And Jesus did not soften the moral seriousness of adultery.
He drove the issue deeper.
He moved from the hotel room to the heart.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” — Matthew 5:27–28
Jesus knew something we desperately try to forget.
The body usually arrives somewhere the heart has already visited.
Long before certain betrayals become physical, something has been rehearsing them internally.
A glance that became a second glance.
A fantasy that was invited back.
A message that should have ended.
A conversation hidden from a spouse.
A friendship that stopped being innocent.
A screen used in darkness.
A secret account.
An emotional attachment defended with the words, “Nothing happened.”
Maybe nothing happened physically.
Yet.
But Jesus cares about what is being cultivated in the heart.
And perhaps that is where somebody reading this needs to stop pretending.
Not tomorrow.
Here.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe your children believe everything is fine.
Maybe the people sitting beside you at church would never imagine what you fight when nobody is looking.
But God knows.
And that sentence can sound terrifying.
Until you remember who came looking for sinners.
Jesus.
The same Christ who warned about lust also stood in a world overflowing with sexually broken, morally compromised, publicly disgraced people.
And He did something astonishing.
He called sinners to repentance…
and offered them mercy.
Not permission.
Mercy.
There is a massive difference.
Grace does not look at chains and call them jewelry.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace does not rename adultery as authenticity.
Grace calls sin what it is so the sinner can finally come home.
Grace does not say, “Keep hiding.”
Grace says, “Come into the light.”
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The Gospel is that your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross.
There, the spotless Son of God bore judgment for sinners.
There, shame met mercy.
There, justice and grace met.
There, Jesus took what guilty people could never erase themselves.
And then He rose.
That means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you have already crossed the line.
Maybe this article found you after the affair.
After the pornography.
After the secret messages.
After the divorce papers.
After the confession.
After your spouse discovered everything.
After your children found out.
After your reputation collapsed.
After you looked into a mirror and barely recognized the person looking back.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that what happened was insignificant.
It tells you something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ is greater than what happened.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is real.
Transformation is possible.
Consequences may remain. Trust may take a long time to rebuild. Some relationships may carry scars.
But scars are not proof that grace failed.
Sometimes scars are evidence that a wound did not kill you.
Peter carried the memory of denying Christ.
Paul carried the memory of persecuting Christians.
The woman at the well carried a complicated relational history.

The Corinthian church contained people whose former lives included serious sexual sin, yet Paul could speak of them as people who had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That little word matters:
were.
That is what some of you need tonight.
Not another excuse.
A were.
I was enslaved.
I was hiding.
I was feeding lust.
I was betraying trust.
I was pretending.
I was living two lives.
But Jesus found me.
Jesus convicted me.
Jesus brought me into the light.
Jesus forgave me.
Jesus began rebuilding what sin had burned down.
And I am not going back.
That is Christianity.
Not respectable people pretending they never became dirty.
Redeemed people pointing toward the One whose blood makes sinners clean.
So if Jeremiah 5:8 exposed something inside you, do not merely feel guilty and keep scrolling.
Repent.
If there is pornography that needs deleting, delete it.
If there is a conversation that needs ending, end it.
If there is an inappropriate relationship being protected by excuses, stop protecting it.
If confession and pastoral accountability are needed, seek them.
If you have sinned against your spouse, do not use “grace” as another hiding place. Genuine repentance does not merely grieve getting caught; it begins turning away from the sin itself.
Bring darkness into the light.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Christ alone saves.
But because the person running toward Jesus cannot simultaneously insist on hugging the chains from which Jesus came to free them.
And if you are the betrayed spouse reading this with tears forming in your eyes…
God sees you too.
Jeremiah's condemnation of adultery means something important for the wounded person.
God does not call betrayal insignificant.
He does not laugh at covenant-breaking.
He does not tell wounded people that their pain is imaginary.
The same God who offers mercy to the repentant sinner is the God who sees the person sinned against.
So do not let somebody weaponize Christian forgiveness to force you into pretending there was no wound.
Healing can take time.
Forgiveness does not make evil good.
Grace does not require calling betrayal harmless.
Jesus can heal both the sinner who truly repents and the wounded heart struggling to understand what happened.
And maybe your struggle is not adultery at all.
Maybe your neighbor's wife is not what you are “neighing” after.
Maybe it is your neighbor's house.
Your neighbor's income.
Your neighbor's marriage.
Your neighbor's ministry.
Your neighbor's body.
Your neighbor's popularity.
Your neighbor's children.
Your neighbor's opportunities.
Your neighbor's life.
Different fence.
Same ancient whisper.
God has not given you enough.
That lie is older than Jeremiah.
It echoes all the way back to Eden.
God surrounded humanity with provision, and the serpent directed attention toward the one forbidden tree.
Look at what you cannot have.
Forget everything God gave you.
Focus on the fence.
And humanity has been staring through fences ever since.
Jeremiah's stallions still run through the human heart.
More.
Someone else.
Something else.
Just once.
Nobody will know.
I deserve this.
I can stop whenever I want.
God will forgive me anyway.
Until appetite becomes master.
And this is precisely why Christianity is not ultimately a program for better self-control.
We need more than stronger fences.
We need a new heart.
We need Christ.
Jesus did not die merely to make badly behaved people slightly more disciplined.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He gives His Spirit.
He transforms desires.
He teaches wandering hearts to say something sin absolutely hates:
Christ is enough.
Enough when temptation whispers.
Enough when loneliness aches.
Enough when marriage is difficult.
Enough when nobody applauds you.
Enough when another person's life looks better through the screen.
Enough when obedience costs something.
Enough when you must choose between feeding an appetite and honoring a covenant.
Jesus is enough.
And when you fall?
Run toward Him in repentance, not away from Him in shame.
Do not wait until you feel clean enough to approach the One who cleans sinners.
Come broken.
Come exposed.
Come without excuses.
Come saying, “Jesus, I did this.”
There is something incredibly liberating about finally stopping the defense attorney inside your head.
No more blaming your spouse.
No more blaming loneliness.
No more blaming stress.
No more blaming alcohol.
No more blaming the algorithm.
No more blaming what somebody sent you.
No more “everybody does it.”
Just truth.
“Lord, I sinned.”
And then grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Resurrection grace.
Grace strong enough to forgive you and holy enough to change you.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to confess private details publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Not because everybody needs another religious post.
Somebody may be one message away from crossing a line.
Somebody may have already crossed it and believes God could never want them again.
Somebody needs Jeremiah's warning before the fall.
Somebody else needs the Gospel after it.
But hear this clearly:
You cannot buy grace.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Give first where Scripture and conscience lead you to give. Care for your family. Support faithful Gospel work. Help people in need.

Financial generosity can glorify God when it flows freely from gratitude and faith rather than pressure. Paul described Christian giving as something decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the kind of support we want.
Not fear.
Not manipulation.
Willing partnership.
Leave a meaningful comment so another struggling believer realizes Christians do not have to pretend.
Save these messages.
Because Gospel ministry is not about building an audience around us.
It is about pointing an audience toward Him.
Back to Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Jeremiah showed us the scandal of hearts fed by God while craving forbidden things.
The Gospel shows us something even more astonishing.
God did not abandon sinners to their appetites.
He sent His Son.
So before you close this article, ask yourself the question you may have been avoiding from the beginning:
What fence have I been staring over while forgetting everything God has already placed before me?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Then look toward Christ.
The Savior who sees the hidden browser history.
The Savior who knows about the deleted messages.
The Savior who knows the fantasy.
The Savior who knows the envy.
The Savior who knows the betrayal.
The Savior who knows what happened behind the closed door.
And still calls sinners to come into the light.
Not so they can remain what they were.
So He can transform them.
Maybe your story contains scandal.
Maybe there are pages you would tear out if you could.
Maybe there are sentences you wish had never been written.
But if you are still breathing, the pen has not reached the final line.
Repent.
Come home.
Follow Jesus.
And remember this when shame whispers that your ugliest chapter gets to name the whole book:
The scandal may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets the final word over the life He redeems.
